query: I am interested in the thermal stability and atomic diffusion behavior of nearly equiatomic high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HENA) composed of five transition metals. What are the fundamental factors governing their structural evolution at elevated temperatures, and how does their behavior compare to traditional alloying concepts? Please propose a hypothesis for their stability, identify relevant prior theoretical constraints, define the boundary conditions where these models might fail, and suggest an experiment to falsify the assumption of intrinsic stability.

generation.hypothesis: Nearly equiatomic high-entropy alloy (HENA) nanoparticles composed of five transition metals exhibit intrinsic thermal stability at elevated temperatures due to the synergistic effects of high configurational entropy, sluggish diffusion kinetics, and severe lattice distortion, which collectively suppress atomic diffusion, phase segregation, and grain growth. However, this stability is conditional on the absence of strong chemical short-range order (SRO) driving forces and is bounded by the nanoparticle size regime where surface energy dominates bulk thermodynamics. At temperatures exceeding 0.6 Tm (melting point), SRO-driven clustering and surface-mediated grain growth will overcome the sluggish diffusion barrier, leading to structural evolution and loss of the single-phase solid solution.
generation.material_initial_state: Nearly equiatomic (5-35 at.% each) HENA nanoparticles (diameter < 50 nm) composed of five transition metals (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi or HfNbTaTiZr) in a disordered single-phase solid solution (FCC or BCC) with high configurational entropy.
generation.intervention: Elevated temperature annealing (0.4–0.8 Tm) in inert or vacuum atmosphere for durations ranging from minutes to hours, followed by characterization of microstructural evolution.
generation.conditions: Temperature range: 0.4–0.8 Tm; Atmosphere: inert/vacuum; Particle size: <50 nm; Time: 10 min to 100 h.
generation.structural_mediator: Chemical short-range order (SRO) clusters and grain boundary mobility, which act as precursors to phase decomposition and grain coarsening.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy stabilizes the disordered solid solution, while sluggish diffusion kinetics (due to severe lattice distortion) retards atomic mobility. However, at elevated temperatures, SRO-driven clustering creates percolation pathways that enhance local diffusion, and surface energy reduction drives grain growth, eventually leading to phase separation or precipitation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Initial stability up to ~0.6 Tm with minimal grain growth or phase decomposition. Beyond 0.6 Tm, SRO clusters will nucleate, followed by grain coarsening and eventual phase separation into intermetallic compounds or elemental-rich regions, particularly in nanoparticles with high surface-to-volume ratios.
generation.baseline: Traditional binary or ternary alloys, which typically exhibit rapid grain growth and phase decomposition at similar temperatures due to lower configurational entropy and faster diffusion kinetics.
generation.boundary: The model fails for nanoparticles with diameters <10 nm (where surface energy dominates) or for compositions with strong negative enthalpy of mixing (promoting intermetallic formation). It also fails under irradiation or mechanical stress, which can accelerate diffusion and phase transformation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature threshold for SRO-driven instability depends on the specific elemental combination and the degree of initial disorder. The role of surface segregation in nanoparticles is not fully quantified in existing literature.
generation.falsification_experiment: Synthesize nearly equiatomic HENA nanoparticles (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi, 20 nm diameter) and anneal them at 0.7 Tm for 10 hours in vacuum. Use in-situ high-resolution TEM and atom probe tomography (APT) to monitor SRO cluster formation and grain growth. If SRO clusters or phase separation are observed within 1 hour, the hypothesis of intrinsic stability is falsified.

First reported in 2004 [ [1] ], high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys comprising five or more elements in equal or nearly equal molar fractions, with each element present at a mole fraction of approximately 5–35 at.% [ [2] ]. The presence of multiple elements leads to a high configurational entropy, resulting in solid-solution structures with face-centred cubic (FCC) and body-centred cubic (BCC) lattices, rather than intermetallic compounds [ [3] ]. In recent years, HEAs have garnered significant consideration in the field of materials science because of their exceptional performance characteristics, including high strength [ [4] ], corrosion resistance [ [5] ], soft magnetic properties [ [6] ], high hardness [ [7] ], wear resistance [ [8] ], fatigue resistance [ [9] ], and softening resistance at high temperatures [ [10] ]. The superior high-temperature behaviour of HEAs can be attributed to four underlying effects: the high entropy effect, the sluggish kinetic diffusion effect, the severe lattice distortion effect, and the cocktail effect [ [11] ].

We study the effects of the chemical short-range order (SRO) on the thermal conductivity of the refractory high-entropy alloy HfNbTaTiZr using atomistic simulation. Samples with different degrees of chemical SRO are prepared by a Monte Carlo scheme. With increasing SRO, a tendency of forming HfTi and TiZr clusters is found. The phonon density of states is determined from the velocity auto-correlation function and chemical SRO modifies the high-frequency part of the phonon density of states. Lattice heat conductivity is calculated by non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations. The heat conductivity of the random alloy is lower than that of the segregated binary alloys. Phonon scattering by SRO precipitates might be expected to reduce scattering times and, therefore, decrease thermal conductivity. We find that, in contrast, due to the increase of the conductivity alongside SRO cluster percolation pathways, SRO increases the lattice heat conductivity by around 12 %. This is expected to be a general result, extending to other HEAs.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides.
